utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Well, Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Appearances for today. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Aditya Menon, and our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson on behalf of the Defence team of General Delic, with assistants Asja Zujo and Lejla Gluhic, legal officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Just to indicate that as you can see, we are just two today. We are sitting 15 bis because Judge Harhoff is sitting in Milosevic. May the Chamber please move into private session -- or just a second, before we do that. Sorry, Mr. Registrar. I'm not quite sure whether we --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're still in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're still in open session. I'm not quite sure if we can do this with the witness still in court. Maybe what we should do -- how long are you likely to be with this witness, madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, between an hour and an hour and an hour and 15 minutes, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask that we excuse the witness for two minutes. There's just a little point that we need to sort out. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber then please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May the witness please be called in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps while the witness is coming in, I will be meeting with the witness that was the subject of that motion over the weekend. And, undoubtedly, he'll ask me, and I'm just curious as to when we might receive a written decision, or if I can orally inform him that those measures will be granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We can perhaps wait until after the completion of this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Mundis -- I beg your pardon, Madam Vidovic. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Begovic.

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, we came to the point where we talked about your moving from the 306th Brigade to the El Mujahedin Unit. I should like you to see another document of the 306th Brigade. I should like you to see another document of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown document D26. This is a document of the 3rd Corps, the number being 02/33-1860 of the 2nd of August, 1993. It is entitled, "Report on Inspection of the 306th Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you to pay attention to this first part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we focus on the first half of the document, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will quote for you a short excerpt from this document. First of all, Witness, as far as I understood, you had no occasion to examine these documents, to see these documents. So I'm not going to ask you about the document, per se, but only in connection with some facts which are referred to in this document, a document of the brigade to which you belonged to approximately up to this time. The date on the document is the 2nd August 1993. Do you agree with that? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to now quote for you a short part of this document, which says: "At the Command of the 306th Brigade in the village of Krpeljici, Lubenovic, the Commander of the 4th Battalion of the 306th Brigade, informed the brigade chief and us that one platoon from Kotor Varos should no longer wish to be part of the strength of the 306th Brigade, and wish to join the 17th Glorious Krajina Brigade immediately. "Also from the Muslim forces station in Mehurici village, a communication was sent to all villages, calling soldiers for a 40-day training. The question of timely rotation of personnel in the Ljuta Greda and Srebrno Brdo, and other centres was raised, and there is also serious problems with soldiers leaving this brigade for the 17th Glorious Krajina Brigade, the Muslim forces in Mehurici village." In regard to this document, I'm going to put a question to you in relation to something I believe you are able to tell us. The sector of Ljuta Greda is an area that you said was covered by precisely your unit prior to your departure from that unit. Is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, partly so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you will agree, will you not, that this document, in fact, demonstrates the actual -- reflects the actual problem in the field? This problem did exist in the field, did it not?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us that there was a disorganization obtaining. If I were to claim that what it in fact was a state of chaos in the military organisation, at that time, in the field, would I be right to qualify it thus?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at any rate, it was a difficult situation due to different things, in addition to the things which you also mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Because the document, again, refers to people leaving the 306th to go to the 17th Brigade, or the Muslim -- to join the Muslim forces in Mehurici. That was the reality; right?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you accept that people in the 306th Brigade were fully aware of the problem of people -- rather fighters leaving the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were probably aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I assert that the 306th Brigade, in fact, had no means of preventing that, would I be right?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that on the basis of my own case. Probably had no resources, had no means with which to prevent such practices.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify what you mean when you say "on my own example, my own case"?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I already said, I went there without leave, without authority. There were no sanctions for me. Now, whether the 306th Brigade had any means to get me to go back to the brigade, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the situation was such that it was either that the 306th Brigade would have to put tens of people in to jail or just simply accept the situation as it was?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't put people in jail then. We had a front line to maintain towards the Army of the Republika Srpska, which was quite a lengthy line; and then, again, there was the portion against the HVO, so people had to maintain the lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I take that to confirm what I am saying. There was no way to prevent these transfers, these moves, rather?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. There wasn't. There was no way to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. We are talking about the 306th Brigade and the time you were there. It did not have an armed military police that could or would carry out such arrests, even if it wanted to arrest people; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is enough. Thank you. Now I should like to quote for you a different small part of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown page 2 of this document. The ERN number is 0182/380 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt you, Madam Vidovic, that document, what do we do with D26?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are still on the same document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The number of the document is 0182-1380.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, I wish to show you the second page of this document. Please be so kind as to take a look at the proposed measures, proposed measures, and Item 4 of that particular paragraph, where it says: "Resolve the problem of the El Jihad formation in Mehurici village in terms of their placement in the establishments of some of the existing brigades or proclaim them paramilitaries (Corps Command-Organ for Mobilisation)." What is your view of this, Witness? The reality was that the 306th Brigade was faced with these problems in the field, the problems with the Arabs, because people joined them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You would agree that the document demonstrates -- and I'll ask you for your opinion, too. The document demonstrates the 306th considered that by placing them within the ABiH, the problems with the Mujahedin would be solved. Does that in fact reflect the reality, in your opinion, because you're a member?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't fully understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question was as follows: The document states that the 306th Brigade suggests that El Jihad be placed within the establishment of the ABiH, that it become part of the ABiH. My question is: Do you agree that this document, in fact, demonstrates that the 306th Brigade had the following position: It thought that by acting in this way, the problems with the Mujahedin would be resolved? Or let me put it this way: Placing the Mujahedin under the control of some formation - it doesn't have to be the 306th Brigade; it could be any formation, any unit in the army - by doing this, the problems could have been resolved? Is that something that everyone was aware of, that all of you in the brigade were aware of, before you transferred?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know much about that. Probably people from the brigade considered that would be a way of solving the problem, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, could we have an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 89.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I hope I won't have to show you a lot of other documents, but, nevertheless, I have two or three more documents to show you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show the witness document D28. The document is from the Security Organ of the 306th Brigade, yet again, and it concerns the people that you were a member from the 20th of May, 1993. The title is "Official Note on the Killing of Atif Brkic, son of Sakib." I'll read out a minor part of the document. It's up on the screen now. Could we highlight the part where we can see the date, the 25th, the 25th of May; and then up until the end of the document, I consider that some of these parts are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'll read out a small part of the document. The document states the following: "On the 25th of May, 1993, a group of Mujahedin, who are not under the control of our brigade and are billeted in Mehurici, that is to say, in the area of responsibility of the 306th Brigade, reconnoitered the Probijeno Brdo sector, elevation 1009, without having asked for permission and without having informed anyone." I'm only interested in this paragraph, so my question is as follows: Your company was in the vicinity of the Mujahedin at the time that this document was drafted; isn't that in fact the case? That's what you said yesterday. And as far as this is concerned, my question is: It's correct to say that the Mujahedin did not request you to provide them with permission to go and reconnoiter; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether they were in my vicinity or not, but I'm familiar with this event. They didn't ask me for anything. I had no contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you're familiar with the event?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you do know, Mr. Atif Brkic, son of Sakib?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean he is deceased. He has died now; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this document conveys information that is correct with regard to what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a conflict between the HVO forces and the Mujahedin, and this young man was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you told us that you were some kind of a company commander there?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You personally never received information of any kind from the Arabs with regard to the results of their reconnoitering?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we have an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number 90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begovic, during your testimony yesterday, you said that your company fought in the Percin area; is that correct? You said you were in the Percin area?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just a minute, let me clarify this. In the course of that action, I was just a simple soldier. I didn't participate in that action with my company, if you understood me. I would just like to correct that. But, yes, I was present there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were present there. Thank you very much. On that occasion, you said that you heard rumours according to which the Arabs had arrived from the direction of Simulje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To our left, that's what was said.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you marked this on the map; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did that yesterday or the day before.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, at the time, you weren't with the Arabs at all; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you didn't see or couldn't observe their movement?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We just heard about the directions they would be going in, but I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when you were testifying, you were, in fact, only assuming the direction that they were heading in; would that be a fair conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Perhaps you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How would you put it? You didn't know the exact direction they were moving in?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I didn't know that it was said that they were be going over through Simulje, in the direction of Borje. I said I can't trace the exact direction, the route on that map, but perhaps the approximate direction. As to the whether it was the exact direction, I don't know, but it was more or less that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. When you say that there were rumours, that this is what you were told, I assume that this isn't something that your commander told you. You heard rumours in the field?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what the troops would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it's not the commander who told you this?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for that clarification. Witness, I will now show you a number of documents that relate to the detachment itself. It has more to do, in fact, with what the Prosecution showed you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown document 67. There seems to be some minor confusion. Not Defence document, but it's Exhibit 67. It was tendered into evidence yesterday, and the number of the first page is 03642916. Yes. Thank you very much. That's the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please have a look at this document once again. It's a document that the Prosecution has already shown you. I'd like us to examine this document in detail. Would you agree with me that it says number 001/93, receipt number, and then there are columns, there are numbers; and then a column that concerns quantity, title, price, and then total at the bottom. It says "Issued by," "Approved by," "Received by." And, Witness, my question about this document is the following: I believe that you have seen a lot of documents on various occasions. I don't just mean documents in this case, but I'm referring to official documents in general. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen a lot of documents. I don't know how many, but I have seen a lot of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You've also seen a lot of receipts that we receive in Bosnia and Herzegovina, when we buy something in shops or when we obtain goods from a warehouse or when we obtain or buy clothes and food. Would you agree that what you have in front of yourself, in fact, looks like a bill from a shop; it doesn't really look like some sort of official document? It mentions prices here, et cetera. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It looks more like something that you'd get from a company of some kind, some kind of equipment from a firm.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. Let's have a look at the second page of the document, 03642917. Have a look at the document, at its contents briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And perhaps the usher could highlight or enlarge the part from number 1 to number 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, or the day before yesterday, when answering the Prosecution's questions, well, you were asked about various individuals. Various names from this list were mentioned, and you were asked about them. You recognised some of them?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in addition to when you were shown photographs, Exhibit number 68, you identified Mr. Abu Aiman, and you said translator. That's the number 11, Deputy Commander for Security, Abu Aiman. You said he was a translator. Isn't it correct to say that while you were in the detachment, he worked as a translator throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, those were the activities he was most involved in. For example, when Sheikh Enver had to come, Abu Maali, well, that's what he was involved in mostly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean --

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this title here, this description.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said you were the emir in a group -- of a group, and it would be logical to conclude that you should know who the Deputy Commander for Security was, if there was such a commander; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you wouldn't agree that it's correct to say that Abu Aiman was the Assistant for Security?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he was a translator; but as to his establishment position, I really don't know what it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness now be shown the third page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The third page, please, have a look at it. It says: "Subject: List of Unit Members." Have a look at the columns. It says, "Number," "First and last name," "Date and place of birth," and then have a look at the last column. It says: "In the ABiH as of." Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you testified at length about the fact that it says here that you were in the army as of the 31st of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown 03642920. It's the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So we have your name there. You found your name there yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, towards the end of the column.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday, the Prosecutor asked you about the date, the 31st of July, and you can see that it concerns membership of the ABiH as of the 31st of July. Isn't it correct to say that you were, in fact, a member of the 306th Brigade from the beginning of the war? So from the very beginning of the war, you were an ABiH member; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So would you agree that this information in this document, according to which you were an ABiH member at the 31st of July, 1993, isn't correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a mistake was made here, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to inform you of the fact that I contest the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was this document not admitted yesterday, madam, or the day before?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. However, I think that we discussed the admissibility of that document at that point. But on the basis of what the witness has said, I doubt its probative value. Actually, I have reason to believe that the document is not authentic, having heard this explanation given by the witness. I shall also require to see the original of this document. And, Your Honours, you will appreciate the fact that the Defence is not always in a position to challenge the authenticity of documents until it has a reason for it, and we have been given just such a reason in the testimony of the witness. So we have two situations: One is the admissibility of the document, and the second is its value, its probity, and its authenticity. Your Honours, if you believe me to be wrong, in future, I shall always ask in advance when a document is being tendered; that is, I shall always take my position with regards its authenticity. But if I am substantiated in my belief that I have to challenge its authenticity by the witness's statement, I believe that I am entitled to do so at any point in the proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, this is actually the first time we've heard a challenge to the authenticity of this document. I'm speaking on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, as was the case with the document that was shown yesterday, in which Mrs. Vidovic challenged the authenticity of the document. And I would simply indicate at this point that if there are going to be challenges to the authenticity of the exhibits on the Prosecution list, I would ask to be informed by the Defence with respect to any and all documents on the Prosecution list that they're challenging with respect to authenticity grounds, so that this problem does not recur. With respect to the original of this document, as I indicated when this question arose from Judge Harhoff, that this document was seized from the Security Services in Zenica in January 2005. With respect to the originals, which Mrs. Vidovic also challenged with respect to a document yesterday, the Prosecution does not have in its possession the originals of these documents. We have scanned versions or photocopy versions. So if Mrs. Vidovic insists upon seeing the originals, she will have to go to the archives in the region in order to do that, because all we have here, with very, very few exceptions, are photocopies or scanned copies of the majority of the documents on the Prosecution exhibit list. So I'm simply alerting the Chamber and the Defence to that issue so that if this becomes a recurring issue, we will be forced to take additional steps, because we don't have the originals, with some exceptions, of course. But this document, we do not have the original. A copy of this was taken from the Security Services in Zenica in January 2005, as I explained two days ago. But, again, if there are going to be recurring challenges to the authenticity of the documents, the Prosecution will submit that that's a bit late, given the stage we're at in these proceedings, when the 65 ter exhibit list was filed on the 31st of October, 2006. And to date, we have not received any specific complaints or any detailed letter in which the Defence have challenged the authenticity of the documents on the Prosecution exhibit list. And, again, this will cause substantial problems, in our respectful view, if this issue continues to arise during the course of the trial. With respect to this specific document, we will simply say that the fact that this witness has indicated that one of the dates on the document might be incorrect does not in any way undermine the authenticity of the document, in light of the fact that the source of the document and how the Office of the Prosecutor came about the document. Minor errors on the face of documents do not necessarily render them inaccurate or unauthentic, I should have said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my apologies. Can I just reply? First and foremost, I believe that the Defence has the right to examine every original and to request to be made available every original which the Prosecution is using against the accused. And, in fact, I believe in your decision on the instruction on conduct during the proceedings that you have given an instruction to that effect. I should like to say this, Your Honours: Of course, we have received the 65 ter list, which contains over 3.000 documents, and, of course, we are investigating each and every document. In every stage of the proceedings, we can come to realise that a document is not authentic, that the document is not authentic, even after judgement has been passed. So we have reason to doubt it, especially if we hear from the mouth of the witness that he's not a lieutenant and the document states that he is a lieutenant, or if there is a different heading on the document, which the witness says is incorrect. That is the best indication for the Defence, which corroborates its doubts. So I believe that this response by the Prosecution is not grounded; namely, that we have to make such objections beforehand, because as often as not we are not in a position to do so. I believe that we can do that at any moment when we obtain valid information to the effect that the document is not authentic. Believe me, Your Honours, we are investigating these documents in earnest, and we shall continue to do so until the proceedings have been validly concluded. It is not up to the Defence to go and investigate the archives, because it is the Prosecution that has actually brought the accused to this dock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a procedural question which neither of you is addressing, which concerns me. I can understand the Defence doubting the authenticity of the document, but to leave a witness in the witness box and now address the question of authenticity seems to me to be procedurally not the right thing to do. I would have expected that you would demonstrate, by your questions to this witness, how you find the document not to be authentic; like the questions you've asked, "You say you were a lieutenant. You were never a lieutenant." I think you also said that the date, 31st of July, 1993, is incorrect. That's fine. You established those facts. And at the time of final submissions, you then address the question of authenticity, because now we have left the witness. We're dealing with something here which the witness has nothing to do with. It's a legal issue that we will resolve at the time. Am I right in this procedural setting out of issues? I'm not talking about the substantive objection. I'm talking about just how to deal with the objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you are quite right. I apologise. I overlooked that and should have asked for the witness to be ushered out of the courtroom. Of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He doesn't have to go out of the courtroom. You carry on with cross-examining him. You get as many facts from him as you can that corroborate your submission that the document is not authentic, and you let him go. At the time of making your final submissions, you then argue that, yes, this document is admitted into evidence; however, it is not authentic for the following reasons, and we ask you to attach little or no probative value to it." I thought procedurally that's how you would handle it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Yes. I have understood this, and this is an instruction that I'm going to abide by in future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the court official now show the witness two documents, the usher, the documents numbers of which are Exhibit numbers 65 and 66. So these are the exhibit numbers that were assigned yesterday. These are not the numbers of the Defence exhibits. Can you just scroll down so the witness can see the date on the document. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Witness, that the date on this document is the 9th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Will you now show Exhibit number 65 -- actually, 66, the next one. This is the same document. Can you show document 65, the document number 65 that was accepted yesterday, dated the 28th of August, 1993. Can we see page 2 of this document, please, and can we see the following page, the next page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please take a look at the date, the 28th of August, 1993. Do you see that date?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you agree that that could have been the time when the official establishment of the El Mujahedin Detachment started? I'm referring to the second half of August 1993. Was that -- was that after you had joined the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was already down there. I was following some training, and I believe that this document is some correspondence between some units, perhaps the 306th Brigade. It is some sort of authorisation, but only after we had already joined them a month later or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. But do we agree that all this was happening after the detachment which was called -- which was given the name El Mujahed, as you said yesterday, did all this take place after that?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I'm going to ask you several questions pertaining to the detachment itself. Would you accept that the detachment, throughout the time that you were a member of it, did not function in the way that other units functioned; for instance, the way the 306th Brigade functioned, in which you had been before that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have already said the organisation was not much. We had combat groups. We had some formations, some units. We composed a company, and the situation in the other units was different.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm reading the transcript. You said first "No," meaning you confirmed that it did not function like the other units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am stressing this, Your Honours, because this is not recorded in the transcript, this part of the witness's answer. That's why I am clarifying it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, the Arabs did have their organisational rules which they were implementing in the detachment, did they not?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, within the detachment it was like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is what I'm asking: Within the detachment?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that they had combat groups which had their emirs?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You, yourself, were an emir, the emir of such a group?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, towards the very end of the war, I was. I was the emir of a group.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that, outside the detachment, no one could join such groups without the emir's authorisation?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand you. Are you talking about combat activities or something else?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking in general. The order had a certain organisational structure, and there was someone in control, the leadership of the detachment was; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So am I right when I say that people just couldn't come and join the detachment from just anywhere, from the road?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. They couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, without authorisation of the leadership of the detachment, no one who was not -- no one unfamiliar and no one who was not invited, called to join the detachment, could do so and go to combat with you?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as the Bosniaks are concerned, they couldn't; but with the Arabs, the situation was different.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will come to that later. I will revert to that later, rather. In giving testimony in responding to the OTP's questions yesterday, you spoke about religious instruction. It was more or less on the same level as the combat instruction was, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite a lot of attention was devoted to religious instruction.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that other units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not have something like that, with perhaps the exception of the 7th Muslim Brigade in a certain period?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they certainly did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You referred to Arabs. They commanded money, had at their disposal money. They bought weapons and equipment for the detachment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you, once again, to look at Exhibit 67, which we already saw before.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This one, I think, was 65 or 66; so 67, please. This document, can we please take a look at page 03642917. Can we zoom in on this note, this annotation on this document, the handwritten annotation. Your Honours, in the translation into English, it is at the very bottom of the English document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we could be shown the very bottom of the English version, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you agree that it is written here, in quite legible handwriting: "Request all data with passport numbers," and indications which country issued the passports. This is actually prompts my next question: You were a member of this detachment ever since its founding until the end of the war; is that correct? That's what you told us?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I was from August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, about that date.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. You would agree with me, would you not, that the Arabs did not use their own names, not even in communicating with other members of the detachment; is that so? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they predominantly had the nicknames that they -- that were given them. What their actual names and their biographies are or were, I don't know, and I don't know if there are any differences between the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be correct to say if I said that not even you, members of the detachment, knew what their real names were?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't know their real names.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't know those names, on the whole, names like Abu something or Ebu something; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that was most frequently the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes, many of them had the same nickname; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were shown the series of photographs, I believe it was Exhibit 68. You were shown a series of photographs, Exhibit 68; and when you were shown these photographs, you identified Abu Hamza.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to save times, Your Honours, I don't think it's necessary to go through the exercise once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you identified this individual, and you said that you knew Abu Hamza. So please tell me, do you agree that many Arabs who were active in Central Bosnia during the war, in fact, had such a nickname?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that's also the case for Abu Zubayr, would you agree with that? There were a number of individuals who had such a nickname? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard about one person.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about a number of such individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given what you said a while ago, when testifying about the Arabs, well, you said, "I know about the Bosnians; they couldn't enter." But as far as the Arabs are concerned, you said, "I know nothing." So it's true that not even you Bosnians in the detachment knew the actual situation? You didn't know the actual number of Arabs who were members of the detachment?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't know. Some would come; others would go. When there was an action of some kind, then a lot of them would arrive. I don't know where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as that's concerned, please tell me the following: There is a detachment that you stayed in. Well, it's true to say that these areas were under the control of the Arabs; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not just under the control of the Arabs. There were guards wherever we had a camp. There were guards. No one could enter without Enver's permission. Even if Rasim Delic had appeared, it would have been necessary for his entry to be authorised.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, regardless of the situation, if a member of the High Command wanted to enter and see something, regardless of that fact, it wouldn't be possible without the emir's authorisation?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Without the emir's authorisation, this would not have been possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the fact that it was someone from the High Command would in no way have been of assistance to that person?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying that it would have been necessary to ask the emir. He couldn't have entered without asking the emir.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that the detachment had its own rules of conduct, which didn't have much to do with the rules and regulations of the ABiH? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, within the detachment, we didn't really adhere to those rules, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'll now go back to the El Mujahedin Detachment. You said you didn't know exactly when it was formed, but I'd like to ask you about something else now. If I have understood you correctly, you joined a group of Arabs, and you fought together with that group. My question is as follows: It would be incorrect to claim that all the Arabs who were active in Central Bosnia joined the El Mujahedin Detachment; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they weren't all in that detachment. There were other people, other individuals, in humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In addition to these people who were in humanitarian organisations, you're referring to Arab humanitarian organisations, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be correct to say that apart from these people, there were many other groups of Arabs that never joined the detachment; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were such groups who didn't agree with the detachment command. There were a few such groups, not just Arabs, though; groups of Turks, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Turkish guerrilla?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Turkish guerrilla from Zenica never joined the El Mujahedin Detachment; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was a group at Gluha Bukovica; were you aware of this group? A group of Arabs - I'm always referring to a group of Arabs - at Gluha Bukovica. Did you know about this group?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was a group at Bistricak?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard about that group.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was a group in Zeljezno Polje?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard about that group, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was a group in Tesanj?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So that group of Arabs also existed, and let's say there was a group in the vicinity of Visoko?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that one.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The groups I have just listed never fought under the command of the El Mujahedin Detachment; am I right?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It would be wrong to assign acts of these groups to the El Mujahedin Detachment; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who you're referring to. Naturally, if they did something, well, this couldn't be attributed to the detachment itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask a question, madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did these groups fight at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this a question for me?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In some areas, yes, these groups did fight, for example. Well, they were always independent and with the army. For the Arabs to fight was like going to a football match.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On whose side did they fight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on the side of the ABiH, on this side over here, on our side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When they did fight, against whom were they fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, against the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were they under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [In English] I have a question. [Interpretation] Witness, since you were fighting the same enemy, the ABiH and the group that you joined, I recognise that is not quite the same thing, but we don't -- we didn't quite know at that time. Was there any single coordination of the operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'll now continue in that vein. When you said that these groups fought on the side of the army, you wanted to say that they were fighting the same enemy?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to say. We were on the same side.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you have no knowledge according to which they were under the control of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. I'm saying that the army and they were on one side. I know nothing about control.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. I'll now move on to another subject, and then I'll come back to the subject of the detachment. From the detachment itself, certain individuals were excluded because they failed to respect the rules and regulations of the detachment; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me if I said that in 1993, there were a number of such cases?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were such cases. One forgets them. A lot of time has passed since then.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They were excluded, and that's quite clear, isn't it, they were excluded, because they failed to abide by the rules of discipline that were in force in the El Mujahedin Detachment; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that many of them continued to fight, although they were not under the control of the El Mujahedin Detachment? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but on the whole they stayed on in Bosnia. I don't know about their fight and how they fought.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Witness. I have a few more questions for you that concern command within the detachment itself, because in the course of your testimony you mentioned a subject. Have I understood you correctly, you said that the detachment had an emir who was above the military commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the command hierarchy. There was the command at two stages, two levels. There was the detachment emir and the military command. As to how that actually worked, well, I don't know exactly. The Presiding Judge asked me about that yesterday, too. I can say that the military commander was involved in military issues, combat action, arms, et cetera. The emir probably had other fields of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me put my question this way: Would it be correct to say that the emir was more influential than the military commander?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certain, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The detachment had an individual who decided or took decisions on all matters of importance; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a body, in fact, within the detachment that took important decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were a member of another kind of unit - that's what you said - before you entered the detachment, before you joined the detachment. As far as you know, command and control in the ABiH didn't have any such bodies or councils or any religious councils, any shuras of this kind; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the army, there was only a deputy commander for morale, who was involved in religious issues to an extent, but it was a different thing. In our detachment, things functioned differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we find out when it's convenient?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In two or three minutes, Your Honours. In two minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I now have something else to ask you about this body or council, this shura. Would I be correct to say that the shura, this body, in fact took decisions as to whether the detachment would engage in combat activity of any kind; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This shura, this body, did take decisions on matters of great importance, that's for certain. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And after August 1993, the shura also decided or continued to decide about matters of importance; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe so, but I didn't have the opportunity of finding out anything about this at the time. I think that this is how things worked until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Witness. We could have a break now. This is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam. We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think we need to go into private session, but I just wanted to say that the decision has been filed. Secondly, I just want to remind the Prosecution about the witness list for next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We earlier had provided a schedule for the entire month of July, and there are no changes to that schedule. I would, for the benefit of the Defence, as well as our own planning, I anticipate filing monthly calendars, if that's acceptable; and then I would -- the default would be if there are no changes, then there's no changes. I would then inform the Chamber and the Defence if there were any changes. But in the absence of any such notification, the schedule, as it stands for the month, will remain the same, if that's acceptable to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's perfectly acceptable. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, also, I would indicate it's certainly our intention to do those monthly schedules by the middle of the preceding month; so that I would hope to have the schedule, for example, for the month of September by the 15th of August, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. I guess the witness may be brought in now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have significantly reduced the number of my questions. I shall only ask for the witness to be shown a photograph from Exhibit number 68. That is from yesterday. This is a photograph with the number - just a minute - 04717273.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, please, you will recall having seen this photograph yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You identified Mr. Sakib Mahmuljin?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Abu Aiman?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Nusret Abdibegovic?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You wrote that down, too. You don't know at all when this photograph was taken; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I only talked about the people on the photograph -- in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the Prosecutor asked you who Sakib Mahmuljin, General Mahmuljin was; and at a certain point, you said that he was the Commander of the 3rd Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said. When I was in the detachment, he was the Commander of the Corps. What he was at this time, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is the purpose of my question. You don't know, at the time when this photograph was taken, whether Mr. Sakib Mahmuljin was the Commander of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Witness. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Vidovic. Mr. Mundis, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour. And, in a moment, I'm going to ask the witness some questions about Exhibit 90, so perhaps that can be pulled up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Begovic, in response earlier this afternoon to some questions from the Defence concerning the shura, I would like to ask you some follow-up questions concerning the Shura Council of the El Mujahedin Detachment. Were you, sir, at that time, while you were in that unit, a member of the Shura of the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On how many occasions, if any, did you ever attend a meeting of the Shura of the EMD or the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, of who exactly were the members --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Let's just get clarity. The question was: "On how many occasions," and you said, "No." De we to understand that by that "no," you to mean that you never attended any of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I never attended any of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, who were the members of the El Mujahedin Detachment Shura at the time you were a member of that unit?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know who were the members. It was probably the people who were in the leadership of the unit that were members of it, but I don't know, with precision, who was on the Shura.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Begovic. I'd now like to show you Exhibit 90, which is a document we looked at a little bit earlier this afternoon, and in particular the last paragraph of this document. Do you see the document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The last paragraph makes reference to the group of Mujahedin that were led by Ramo Durmis from Zenica. Do you know Ramo Durmis?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber who Ramo Durmis was or is?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I joined the detachment, he was just a simple soldier, as far as I know. What he did before that, I don't know. But he was said to be some sort of a leader, perhaps the emir of a group, before I came, that is. I don't know whether he was with the detachment throughout the war. I can't say that with precision, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This document, sir, that you have before you, indicates he's currently "the Commander of the Bosniaks among the Mujahedin in Mehuric." Can you comment on that phrase that's contained in Exhibit 90?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The only thing that I can say is that he was perhaps the leader of a group of Bosniaks. I don't know how else I could comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Begovic, if Ramo Durmis had a nickname, or if he went by any "Abu" nicknames in particular?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Begovic. The Prosecution has no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. Judge Lattanzi? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said there were two leaders of the detachment: There was the military commander and the emir. As to the military commander, was he Bosnian or was he a foreigner?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a foreigner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You added that the emir would participate in taking major decisions, and also when it came to operations or actions, as you stated two days ago. So these were military decisions, but were there also decisions having to do with the organisation within the detachment only?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably there also were. Within the detachment, the organisation was a bit specific, as it were. For instance, in the Vastrostalna in Zenica, we had the Medresa, the religious instruction segment, and then we had the fitness training and the handling of weapons training in other places. So they probably looked after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But they would also make decisions with regard to military operations or actions?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They certainly participated in the adoption of such decisions, together with the military emir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge Lattanzi. Let me just start with this Exhibit 90, which was here, Mr. Begovic, before we forget about it. Let me say, when you joined the El Mujahedin, was Mr. Ramo Durmis already a member or did he join after you?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was already there before I joined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you testified over the last three days about the engagement of your detachment in battle. The question I want to ask you is: While you were involved in war, were there any time where your group or your side captured any prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I didn't. My group didn't have any captured combatants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you, at any time, aware of any prisoners of war that may have been captured by any of the groups on your side?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We later heard that some people had been captured in the second action, but I believe that an exchange took place, so that I did not feel the need to talk about it. But I, personally, and my group did not capture anyone. I believe these other people were captured by the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean "they were captured by the army"?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am referring to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, someone from the 2nd Brigade. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say you heard that they were -- well, they probably got exchanged. Do you know what happened to them between the time of their capture and the time of their exchange?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have occasion to see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll leave the question of prisoners of war. Were you aware of -- let me rephrase that question. To your knowledge, where did the group that you belonged to receive its instructions from, if any?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does this question refer to, to the action or to the peace-time conditions when there were no combat operations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm talking about when there were combat operations.

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see. We got our instructions from the military emir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand. But the military emir, you're talking about the emir of your group, isn't it so, your unit?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was referring to Muatez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question to you is: Are you aware of whether at all Muatez received instruction from anybody else?

utterances.speaker: SINAN BEGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Begovic. I have no further questions for you. Any questions arising from the questions by the Bench, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Begovic, this brings us to the end of your testimony. The Trial Chamber would like to thank you very much for coming to testify, taking time off your very busy schedule, and you are now excused. You may leave. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before we call the next witness, I just wanted to clear up one issue from yesterday. The Trial Chamber will recall, with respect to the video which had been marked for identification as Exhibit 81, and the corresponding transcript which was Exhibit 82 marked for identification, we indicated that we wanted the opportunity to review the transcript of that videotape. I have had the opportunity to do so, and at this point in time the Prosecution has no objection to Exhibit 81, the video, and the corresponding transcript, 82, being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. Exhibits 81 and 82 that were marked for identification yesterday are now admitted into evidence and as exhibits. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Hasib Alic, and my colleague, Laurie Sartorio, will be conducting the direct examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I rise just to make one point before we start with the next witness. I'd just like to draw to the Court's attention that on our return from the break at 4.00 p.m., I found at my desk a new witness statement for this witness. It's nine pages long and some 43 paragraphs in length. The next witness is, rather like Mr. Begovic, a former member of the El Mujahed Detachment. His evidence covers the whole span of the indictment from 1993 to 1995. And I note, from a brief perusal of the statement, that within the statement, there are several aspects of his evidence which are materially different from the former statement that we have. It's therefore the case, Your Honour, that I feel a little uncomfortable dealing with the cross-examination today without having a proper opportunity to study the new and detailed statement. Your Honour, I note that the court time is precious. It's 20 past 4.00 now, and I would anticipate that the examination-in-chief would probably take us just some time beyond the next break. We'll be breaking, I guess, from 5.30 to 6.00. So with the Court's permission, Your Honour, it's my application that we adjourn a little bit earlier and deal with the cross-examination first thing on Monday morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio, is there any reason for the Defence to be given a different statement so late in the day?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, this statement was the result of the proofing of the witness. The witness wanted to make some corrections to his first statement, and he also had some substantive additions to additions to add to his testimony, so I felt it was my obligation to have a new statement drafted up, and the witness was read the statement back in his own language and he signed the statement. So I had to disclose it. But it's purely as a result of the proofing. I've spent several hours with this witness over the past two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is there a possibility of avoiding a recurrence of this nature?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, the policy of the OTP is that witnesses are brought in just a few days before their testimony. So if there is another way, Your Honour, we would be more than amenable to using that method. It's the Victim Witness Unit, Your Honour, that decides the time frame, so it's really beyond the power of the OTP to ask or require a witness to come in several days before his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a comment to make. Well, I choke on it, so I'd rather not make it. Okay. Thank you very much. But do you have any objection to this witness being cross-examined next week?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I don't have any objection, Your Honour. I don't know what the witness's position is, what his situation is at home, whether he has to return today and return on Sunday. I'm not sure. We'll have to speak with the witness after his testimony today. I hope to be completed, Your Honour, within an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but your opposite number is not ready, precisely because of the statement that they've just received. So they will not be in a position to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You understand that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Well, then you can cross-examine on Monday, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think arrangements shall have to be made for the accommodation and proper care of the witness over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Mr. Hasib Alic to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Alic. You may be seated. Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, what country are you from?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: From Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And in 1990 and 1991, were you also in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: What were you doing during those two years, in terms of occupation?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Were you a soldier in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That was in 1990/1991?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, in 1992, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: In 1992, well, nothing. Farm work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Excuse me. Sorry. I didn't hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I heard the interpretation say, "Nothing. Farm work."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, when do you believe the war started in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that there were village guards on the 4th of April, 1992; and then perhaps a month or two later, things became a little more intense.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And during that time, were you a member of the armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what unit were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: Well, when I look back, I was a member of the ABiH from the beginning, from the 4th of April, as it is stated in my military booklet, up until the 14th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. 4th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I think there's some confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: You, according to your military booklet, you became a member of the Army for Bosnia-Herzegovina in April of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: According to my military booklet, it was on the 4th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Excuse me. Sorry. Yes. And what was your role in the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: Not much of a role.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, were you a part of a unit, a brigade?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time at the beginning, there was no such thing, but later there was the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you were a member of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And were you carrying out some operations during your time in 1992 and early 1993 with the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, what were you doing in the armed forces? What kind of work were you doing? Reconnaissance?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: On the whole, I stood guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, at some point in 1993, did you move into another unit?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And -- excuse me. And what was the name of that unit?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: The El Mujahed Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And why did you move into that unit?

utterances.speaker: HASIB ALIC
utterances.text: Well, I thought it would be better for me.
